hook: A hawk does not eat just one thing, and neither does a fox or a frog. Draw every feeding link in a meadow and you get a tangled web, not a straight line. That web is why ecosystems can absorb some losses, and why removing one key species can still change everything around it.

prereq.q: About what share of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?

figure.caption: A meadow food web: arrows point from food to eater.

chain.cause: Most organisms eat several foods and are eaten by several predators
chain.effect: food chains link into a food web
its predators switch to other prey, and its prey increase
species two or three steps away can change too

ideas: A food chain is one path of who eats whom; a food web is all the linked chains in an ecosystem.
Arrows point from food to eater, the way energy and matter move.
Decomposers and detritivores break down dead matter from every level and return nutrients to producers.
Webs with many links are usually more stable: consumers can switch food when one species declines.

misconception.wrong: Removing a predator only affects the species it eats.
misconception.right: Effects spread through the web. Fewer predators means more of their prey, which then eat more of their own food: a change can reach producers two or three links away.

summary: A food chain follows one path of energy from producers to top consumers; a food web shows all the overlapping chains in an ecosystem. Arrows point from food to eater. Decomposers and detritivores recycle nutrients from every level. Because organisms are linked, a change in one population spreads: prey increase when predators decline, and the effect can reach plants several links away.
